title: Edge cases, invalid input and error paths
learningObjectives: Distinguish valid ordinary input, boundary input, invalid input and operational failure.
Identify empty, minimum, maximum, duplicate and out-of-range cases relevant to a problem's contract.
Validate input conversions and check library return values before using produced data.
Design explicit error paths that avoid continuing with incomplete or invalid state.
Prevent array-bound violations, arithmetic overflow and invalid pointer use when handling unusual inputs.
Document and test the program's behaviour for every defined failure and boundary condition.

understand.concept: An edge case is an input or state near a boundary of the problem's rules; invalid input violates those rules. An error path is the deliberate route the program follows when an operation cannot safely continue. Reliable programs define these behaviours instead of hoping unusual cases never occur.
understand.whyItMatters: Many serious defects occur at boundaries: empty arrays, zero quantities, maximum values, malformed text, failed file opens or failed allocations. Explicit checks prevent invalid data from reaching code that assumes it is valid.
understand.analogy: A building entrance checks tickets and handles cases such as a missing ticket, an expired ticket or a full venue. The normal entrance path is only one of several outcomes that must be planned.
understand.analogyLimit: Not every unusual input is invalid. A zero-length collection may be a valid case. The specification decides which values are allowed and what result each case requires.

explain.narrative:
Derive edge cases from the contract. For a count, consider zero, one and the largest supported value. For a range, test just below, at and just above each boundary. For text input, consider empty lines, extra characters, malformed numbers and values outside the destination type. For arrays, ensure every index is less than the element count.

Check every operation that can fail. scanf-family functions return the number of successful assignments; fgets returns NULL on failure or end-of-file; fopen can return NULL; malloc can return NULL. Do not read an output variable or dereference a pointer until success has been established. For numeric text, strtol with errno and an end pointer provides more control than assuming a conversion succeeded.

Make error handling part of the design. Return a status, preserve a valid prior state, release resources already acquired and avoid printing a success message after a failed operation. Define whether invalid input is rejected, retried or replaced with a default; never choose silently when the requirement does not say.

examples.title: Parse an integer line and reject malformed or out-of-range input
examples.explanation: The program checks whether a line was read, whether any digits were converted, whether strtol reported range error, whether the value fits int and whether non-whitespace characters remain. A fixed buffer also means an overlong line needs an explicit policy in production; this example rejects trailing content in the captured line.

examples.title: Treat an empty collection as a defined case
examples.explanation: The function explicitly rejects a missing output pointer, a missing input array for a nonempty collection and an empty collection because an average is undefined for zero items. A production contract should also bound count so the long long sum cannot overflow.

practise.guidedTask: For a program that divides one integer by another, list cases for divisor zero, positive and negative values, minimum/maximum inputs and malformed text. Decide which are valid and specify each result.
practise.independentTask: Write a robust function that searches an array. Define behaviour for zero elements, a null pointer with a nonzero count, an absent target and a count that cannot be represented by the chosen return type. Add explicit error handling and tests.
hints: Do not assume an empty collection is invalid; consult the problem definition.
Check library return values before using output parameters or pointers.
For strtol, inspect end, errno and the destination type's range.
Check bounds before indexing; checking after access is too late.
Do not continue a calculation after a required input or allocation failed.
Choose and document whether the program rejects, retries or recovers from invalid input.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an edge case is correct?
options: It is a boundary or unusual case whose expected behaviour should be defined
It can be ignored if the normal example works
It is necessarily a compiler error
questions.answer: It is a boundary or unusual case whose expected behaviour should be defined
questions.explanation: An edge case may be valid or invalid; its expected behaviour comes from the specification.

questions.prompt: What should be checked after calling strtol?
options: The end pointer, errno and whether the value fits the destination type
Only whether the returned value is nonzero
Nothing if the input came from stdin
questions.answer: The end pointer, errno and whether the value fits the destination type
questions.explanation: These checks detect no conversion, range errors and trailing or out-of-range values.

questions.prompt: What does fopen return when a file cannot be opened?
questions.explanation: fopen reports failure with a null pointer, which must be checked before using the stream.

questions.prompt: When is it safe to access values[i] in an array of count elements?
options: After establishing that i is less than count and the array is valid
questions.answer: After establishing that i is less than count and the array is valid
questions.explanation: The valid index range is 0 through count - 1, provided the array object contains count elements.

questions.prompt: What is a sound error-path design?
options: Report or return failure, preserve valid state and release acquired resources
Print success regardless of the operation result
questions.answer: Report or return failure, preserve valid state and release acquired resources
questions.explanation: A failure path must prevent unsafe continuation and account for resources already acquired.
